summary: Reproduces FIPS 98, a specification for message format for computer based message systems, to make it accessible to the ARPA research community. It does not specify an ARPA Internet standard and replaces RFC 806.

eli5.summary: A government rulebook for how electronic messages should look, shared so researchers could read it.

questions: what fields are required in a cbms message
what is a user agent in a message system
subtitle: A US federal standard for what goes inside an electronic message, republished as an RFC for ARPA researchers.

tldr.problem: Different computer-based message systems each stored and structured messages their own way, so users of one system could not reliably exchange messages with users of another.
tldr.mechanism: FIPS 98 defines a message as a set of named fields (From, To, Posted-Date, Subject, Text and more) and a compact binary encoding of nested data elements, each with an identifier octet, a length code and contents.
tldr.outcome: It is the National Bureau of Standards' message format standard, reproduced as RFC 841 and replacing RFC 806. The RFC itself states that it does not specify a standard for the ARPA Internet.

today: RFC 841 is the NBS standard FIPS 98 reproduced for the ARPA community, and it replaces RFC 806. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC itself says it does not specify an ARPA Internet standard.

sections.title: What FIPS 98 Is and Why It Is an RFC
sections.content:
RFC 841 reproduces FIPS Pub 98, Message Format for Computer Based Message Systems, issued by the National Bureau of Standards on 27 January 1983. The RFC says it was distributed only to make the document easy to reach for the ARPA research community, and that it does not specify a standard for the ARPA Internet.

A computer-based message system (CBMS) lets people (or roles, or processes) send messages through computers, with tools to write them and to process them after arrival. The standard exists so that users of different CBMSs can send messages to each other. It applies to Federal departments and agencies buying or using such systems in networked settings. Stand-alone systems and networks set up purely for computer science or communications research are exempt.
sections.eli5: Different mail programs wrote their letters in different ways. This book says how everybody should write them so letters can be read anywhere.

sections.title: What Is In and Out of Scope
sections.content:
The specification defines the meaning and form of standard fields, which fields must be in every message, which fields a complying system must be able to process, and how messages, fields and field data are represented.

It deliberately leaves out many things: the message transfer system and its protocols, message envelopes, how unique identifiers and message IDs are written, network addressing, how originators and recipients are named, text editing, how messages are shown to users and stored internally, and multi-media representations. The standard only constrains the message format at the interface between systems. A system converts to the standard format when a message leaves and back to its own format when one arrives.

The format is not a protocol. It describes data used by an application, which would be handled by a layer 7 (Application) protocol in the OSI model.
sections.eli5: The book only says what the letter inside looks like. It says nothing about the envelope, the stamp or the mail truck.

sections.title: The Model of a Message System
sections.content:
The RFC borrows a logical model developed by IFIP Working Group 6.5. It has one Message Transfer System (MTS) and a number of User Agents (UAs). A User Agent acts on behalf of a user to create and process messages. The MTS accepts a message from the originator's User Agent and passes it on to each recipient's User Agent, doing routing and storage along the way if needed.

Handing a message to the MTS is Posting; handing it to a recipient's User Agent is Delivery. The point where responsibility changes hands is called a Slot. A message splits into its content, which this standard defines, and its envelope, which it does not. The MTS is expected to carry messages without reading or altering them unless a User Agent tells it to.

Originators and recipients can be people, roles (such as a city desk at a newspaper), processes, or, for recipients, groups, which are predefined lists of recipients.
sections.eli5: You hand your letter to the post office, and the post office hands it to your friend. The post office never opens it.

sections.title: Messages and Their Fields
sections.content:
A message is a series of fields. Valid messages must contain one From field, one To field and one Posted-Date field. Each field belongs to a compliance category: REQUIRED fields must be in every message and processed by receivers, BASIC fields may be absent but must be processed when present, and OPTIONAL fields may be ignored, though receivers must not treat them as errors.

  • Originator: From (REQUIRED), Reply-To (BASIC), Author and Sender (OPTIONAL).
  • Recipient: To (REQUIRED), Cc (BASIC), Bcc, Circulate-To and Circulate-Next (OPTIONAL).
  • Dates: Posted-Date (REQUIRED), plus optional Date, Start-Date, End-Date, Received-Date and Warning-Date.
  • Cross-reference: Message-ID, In-Reply-To, References, Obsoletes and Originator-Serial-Number, all OPTIONAL.
  • Handling and content: Precedence, Message-Class, Reissue-Type and Received-From (OPTIONAL), then Subject and Text (BASIC), and Attachments, Comments and Keywords (OPTIONAL).

The Date field is to Posted-Date as the date on a letter is to the postmark. Fields not defined by the standard are vendor-defined fields, and fields from a formal extension are extension fields.
sections.eli5: A message is a form with boxes: who it is from, who it is for, the date, a subject and the text. Three boxes must always be filled in.

sections.title: Reissuing, Replies and Life Spans
sections.content:
The standard describes how fields support common functions. The people involved in sending can differ: the Author writes, the From person takes responsibility, and the Sender actually posts it, as when a secretary posts for a manager.

Forwarding is informal: a system copies the old message into a field of a new one, so the original may lose its message structure. Reissuing is formal: the whole original message is embedded inside a new message, so it can always be pulled out as a well-formed message. The Reissue-Type field tells the two purposes apart: Redistribution (sending the unchanged message to new recipients, with the ASCII string Redistribution) and Assignment (delegating responsibility). Reissuing can nest to any depth.

Other fields serve reply generation (Reply-To, falling back on From), cross-referencing, and life span functions through Start-Date, End-Date and Warning-Date. The specification does not say exactly how a Bcc list must be shown to recipients.
sections.eli5: Forwarding is copying a letter onto new paper. Reissuing is putting the whole original letter inside a new envelope, so nothing changes.

sections.title: How Messages Are Encoded
sections.content:
Messages are built from data elements. Primitive elements hold plain data (such as ASCII-String, Integer, Bit-String and Boolean), while constructor elements such as Message, Field, Sequence and Set contain other elements. The specification defines nineteen data elements. A Message may hold only Field elements, other Message elements, or encrypted or compressed forms of them, and Compressed and Encrypted elements exist for those purposes.

Every data element is made of up to five components, always in this order: an identifier octet, a length code, a qualifier, a property list and the contents. Bit 7 of the identifier octet says whether properties are attached and bit 6 says whether a qualifier follows. The other seven bits identify the element.

Length codes come in three forms. A short code is one octet with a value of 0 through 127. A long code starts with an octet whose top bit is 1 and whose other seven bits say how many octets hold the value. An indefinite code is a single octet 10000000 and may appear only in constructors, which then end with an End-Of-Constructor element. Systems must handle length codes and qualifiers expressed in three octets or fewer.

Properties are extras that do not change meaning. The two defined ones are Printing-Name (a display label) and Comment. Vendors can define their own qualifiers and data elements, but these are not guaranteed to be unique and should be used by prior agreement.
sections.eli5: Every piece of the message is wrapped in a little label saying what it is and how long it is, like boxes inside boxes, so a computer knows where each one ends.

data.title: A redistributed message
data.code:
Message:
  Field: From "John Doe"
  Field: Posted-Date "28 January 1983"
  Field: To "Jane Jones"
  Field: Reissue-Type "Redistribution"
  Message:
    Field: From "Jean Smith"
    Field: Posted-Date "27 January 1983"
    Field: To "John Doe"
    Field: Subject "Next Project Meeting"
    Field: Text "The agenda for ..."
